profile.overview:
Sahajanand Medical Technologies Limited develops, manufactures, and sells medical devices used in vascular and structural heart interventions. Founded in 2001, the company offers vascular intervention products, including coronary stents and coronary balloon catheters, and structural heart products, including transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) devices and occluders. Its portfolio also includes renal stents, peripheral drug-coated balloons, and traded medical products.
The company markets its products through direct sales, hybrid, and distributor-led models. In FY26, it generated revenue from 77 countries, including India, with operations across Europe and other international markets. It currently operates three manufacturing facilities, two in India and one in Thailand. Additionally, it has two research and development centres, located in India and Thailand, focused on medical device development and product improvements.
Use of proceeds: 
The IPO is an offer-for-sale (OFS). The company will not receive any proceeds from the offer. Net proceeds from the offer will go to the promoter selling shareholders in proportion to the number of shares offered by them for sale.
The primary objective of the offer is to achieve the benefits of listing the equity shares on the stock exchanges, which is expected to enhance the company’s visibility and brand recognition. Listing will also provide liquidity to the existing shareholders and create a public market for the company’s shares in India​.
profile.productsAndServices: Sahajanand Medical Technologies Ltd operates in Healthcare (Founded 1999).
profile.businessModel: Mainboard issue (EQUITY) listed on NSE / BSE · ISIN INE356Y01018.
profile.industryOverview: Healthcare primary market offering tracked via SEBI & exchange filings.
strengths: According to the F&S Report, Sahajanand Medical Technologies held nearly 25% of India's drug-eluting stents (DES) market by sales volume in FY26. The company was also among the top five by DES sales volume in Germany, Spain, Poland, and Brazil as of March 31, 2026.

The company marketed its products in 77 countries, including India, in FY26. Its international revenue from operations increased from Rs 587.84 crore in FY24 to Rs 704.23 crore in FY25 and Rs 894.20 crore in FY26, representing a CAGR of 23.34%.

The company operates two R&D centres in Surat, India, and Nonthaburi, Thailand. As of the RHP date, it had 119 granted patents globally, 78 pending patent applications, and five design registrations in India. Its R&D expenditure stood at 9.04%, 9.07%, and 8.61% of revenue from operations in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively.

The company claims to have an extensive clinical research portfolio supporting its medical devices. As of June 30, 2026, its products were supported by 75 clinical studies, including 66 completed and nine ongoing studies, with research on its products published in medical journals such as The Lancet and The New England Journal of Medicine.

The company operates three manufacturing facilities in Surat, Hyderabad, and Thailand. All three facilities hold ISO 13485:2016 certification for medical device quality management systems. Its facilities also hold various regulatory approvals and certifications, including CDSCO, CE, ANVISA, TGA Australia, and Korean GMP, depending on the facility.

The company claims to have integrated manufacturing capabilities, including in-house production of balloon catheters, laser cutting, electropolishing, drug and polymer coating, and valve manufacturing. It also reported that approximately 33% of the available area at its Hyderabad facility was being utilised, providing space for future expansion.

The company has completed acquisitions to expand its product portfolio and international distribution network. Its acquisitions of Vascular Concepts and Vascular Innovations enabled its entry into structural heart devices, while the acquisitions of Imex in Spain and Zarek in Brazil strengthened its distribution operations. Revenue from Imex and Zarek grew at CAGRs of 52.10% and 23.91%, respectively, since their acquisition in FY20.
risks: The company's revenue from vascular intervention (VI) devices stood at Rs 618.27 crore (68.57%), Rs 674.97 crore (65.86%), and Rs 740.09 crore (61.14%) in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Additionally, its Supraflex Cruz product contributed Rs 431.35 crore (47.84%), Rs 431.03 crore (42.06%), and Rs 450.00 crore (37.17%) to revenue from operations during the same periods, respectively. Any decline in demand for these products or increased competition could adversely affect the company's revenue and profitability.

The company's top 10 suppliers accounted for purchases worth Rs 164.57 crore (58.88%), Rs 170.75 crore (64.37%), and Rs 184.72 crore (59.15%) in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. The company also depends on a limited number of suppliers, including single suppliers for certain critical materials, and does not enter into long-term supply agreements. Any supply disruption or increase in raw material prices could adversely affect its manufacturing operations and profitability.

The company's imports accounted for Rs 207.60 crore (74.28%), Rs 195.41 crore (73.67%), and Rs 241.00 crore (77.18%) of its total purchases in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Its dependence on imported raw materials and components from countries including Germany, China, the Netherlands, and Ireland exposes it to foreign exchange fluctuations, import restrictions, and supply chain disruptions, which could negatively impact its operations and financial performance.

The company's revenue from customers outside India stood at Rs 587.84 crore (65.20%), Rs 704.23 crore (68.71%), and Rs 894.20 crore (73.87%) in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Since a significant portion of its revenue and purchases is denominated in foreign currencies, adverse exchange rate movements could affect its profitability and financial condition.

The company's top 10 distributors contributed Rs 237.47 crore (26.34%), Rs 215.34 crore (21.01%), and Rs 190.12 crore (15.71%) to revenue from operations in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. The company generally does not enter into long-term agreements with its distributors, and certain international product registrations are held in their names. Any loss of key distributors or termination of these arrangements could adversely affect its sales and market presence.

The company has experienced underutilisation of certain manufacturing capacities. In FY26, capacity utilisation for stents at its Hyderabad facility stood at 64.26%, while utilisation for drug-coated PTCA balloon catheters at its Surat facility was just 1.81%. Continued underutilisation of manufacturing facilities could increase operating costs and adversely affect the company's profitability.

The company has faced regulatory challenges in certain international markets. Its subsidiary in Brazil had a product registration cancelled following a classification dispute, while its applications for Hydra TAVI in Taiwan and Australia were rejected and required additional testing or clinical studies. Any delay or failure in obtaining the required regulatory approvals could restrict the company's ability to sell its products in these markets.

The company has received notices from regulatory authorities regarding its operations. Its subsidiary received a notice from the Telangana Pollution Control Board in December 2024 concerning effluent disposal, while the company received a notice from the Assistant Drug Controller and Licensing Authority in May 2024 regarding discrepancies at its premises, with the latter matter remaining pending as disclosed in the RHP. Any adverse regulatory action could result in penalties, suspension of licences or disruption of manufacturing operations.

The company reported a consolidated loss of Rs 7.35 crore in FY24 and standalone losses of Rs 34.46 crore and Rs 7.92 crore in FY24 and FY25, respectively. Additionally, certain subsidiaries, including SMT Switzerland AG and Vascular Innovations Co Ltd have reported losses in recent periods. Continued losses at these entities could require additional financial support from the company and adversely affect its consolidated financial position.

The company's average working capital stood at Rs 263.91 crore, Rs 254.25 crore, and Rs 291.44 crore in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. As of June 30, 2026, it had outstanding working capital loans amounting to Rs 240.99 crore. Inability to generate sufficient internal funds or obtain additional working capital financing could adversely affect its operations and financial condition.

The company incurred substantial research and development expenditure amounting to Rs 81.46 crore (9.04%), Rs 92.99 crore (9.07%), and Rs 104.16 crore (8.61%) of revenue from operations in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Any failure to successfully develop, obtain regulatory approval for or commercialise new products could result in unrecovered R&D expenditure and adversely affect the company's profitability.

The company's trade receivables stood at Rs 215.17 crore, Rs 263.48 crore, and Rs 286.25 crore as of March 31, 2024, 2025, and 2026, respectively. As of June 30, 2026, its trade receivables stood at Rs 306.56 crore. Any delay or default in receiving payments from customers or distributors could adversely affect the company's cash flows, profitability and financial condition.

The company, its subsidiaries, directors, and promoters are involved in certain outstanding legal proceedings. Any adverse judgments in these cases could negatively impact the company's business, reputation and financial position
As of June 30, 2026, the company had outstanding financial indebtedness of Rs 320.63 crore. Any failure to service or repay these loans can harm the company’s operations and financial position.

profile.overview:
Tonbo Imaging India Limited is a defence electronics original equipment manufacturer (OEM) engaged in the design, development, and manufacturing of sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems for defence and security applications.
The company's product portfolio is divided into tactical systems and platform systems. Its products include thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems, missile guidance systems, and surveillance equipment. These products are used in surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and control applications. The company supplies its products to government defence agencies, law enforcement and homeland security agencies, and other defence equipment manufacturers in India and overseas.
The company operates an R&D centre in Bengaluru, Karnataka, where it undertakes product design, development and prototyping. It follows an asset-light manufacturing model, outsourcing production to electronics manufacturing services partners, including Kaynes Technology India Limited and Avalon Technology and Services Private Limited.
Use of proceeds: 
The IPO is an offer-for-sale (OFS). The company will not receive any proceeds from the offer. Net proceeds from the offer will go to the selling shareholders in proportion to the number of shares offered by them for sale.
The primary objective of the offer is to achieve the benefits of listing the equity shares on the stock exchanges, which is expected to enhance the company’s visibility and brand recognition. Listing will also provide liquidity to the existing shareholders and create a public market for the company’s shares in India.
profile.productsAndServices: Tonbo Imaging India Ltd operates in Aerospace & Defence (Founded 2003).
profile.businessModel: Mainboard issue (EQUITY) listed on NSE / BSE · ISIN INE0LDG01026.
profile.industryOverview: Aerospace & Defence primary market offering tracked via SEBI & exchange filings.
strengths: As per the F&S Report, Tonbo Imaging India Limited was the largest manufacturer of thermal imaging systems supplied to government and defence agencies in India by sales value between April 2024 and March 2026. The company also accounted for 94% of India's thermal imaging exports by units during this period.

As of June 30, 2026, the company had deployed over 28,000 tactical systems across 24 countries. Its products have been supplied to defence and security customers in markets including India, the USA, Romania, Armenia, South Korea, the UAE, and Australia.

The company claims to own 100% of the intellectual property used in its products since FY24, following the acquisition of intellectual property worth Rs 183.19 crore from CEAQ Singapore in March 2024. Its technologies cover infrared imaging, optics, embedded software, AI-based image processing and electronic systems.

The company operates an R&D centre in Bengaluru, which employs 130 engineers, representing 38.35% of its workforce as of June 30, 2026. Its R&D expenditure increased from Rs 4.24 crore in FY24 to Rs 9.09 crore in FY25 and Rs 25.86 crore in FY26.

The company follows an asset-light manufacturing model, outsourcing production to electronics manufacturing services partners, including Kaynes Technology India Limited and Avalon Technology and Services Private Limited. It retains in-house control over product design, development and core technologies.

The company's R&D centre is ISO 9001:2015 certified for quality management systems, ISO 14001:2015 for environmental management systems, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 for information security management systems, and ISO 28000:2022 for security and resilience management systems.

The company offers a diversified portfolio of tactical and platform systems used in ground, aerial, naval, and missile applications. Its products include thermal weapon sights, handheld imaging systems, stabilised multi-sensor gimbals, fire control systems and missile seekers, serving different defence operational requirements.
risks: The company's revenue from operations stood at Rs 428.19 crore, Rs 469.08 crore, and Rs 362.65 crore in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively, recording a decline of 22.69% in FY26. The decline was primarily attributed to delays in international orders arising from the West Asia conflict and the deferment of certain anticipated orders to FY27.

The company's top 10 customers contributed Rs 361.81 crore (84.50%), Rs 447.92 crore (95.49%), and Rs 282.22 crore (77.83%) to its revenue from operations in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Any failure to retain these key customers, expand its customer base, or secure new contracts could adversely affect the company's business and financial standing.

The company's top 10 suppliers accounted for Rs 227.39 crore (67.49%), Rs 132.74 crore (35.46%), and Rs 206.27 crore (68.77%) of its total expenses in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. The company does not have long-term agreements with its raw material suppliers, and any disruption in these relationships could adversely affect its operations.

The company relies on a limited number of international suppliers for critical components such as infrared sensors, OLED microdisplays, and specialised optics. Procurement of critical components from international suppliers amounted to Rs 90.67 crore, Rs 107.34 crore, and Rs 97.05 crore in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Any export restrictions, supply disruptions or price increases could adversely affect its production and profitability.

The company's revenue from customers located outside India stood at Rs 208.15 crore (48.61%), Rs 307.34 crore (65.52%), and Rs 20.21 crore (5.57%) in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Any adverse political, economic, or regulatory developments in its export markets, particularly Europe, could negatively impact its business and financial performance.

The company derives a significant portion of its revenue from tactical systems, which contributed Rs 359.27 crore (83.90%), Rs 362.30 crore (77.24%), and Rs 211.67 crore (58.37%) to revenue from operations in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively. Any decline in demand for these products could adversely affect its revenue and profitability.

The company recorded negative cash flows from operating activities amounting to Rs 136.12 crore and Rs 63.22 crore in FY25 and FY26, respectively, and Rs 14.68 crore in the three months ended June 30, 2026. The negative cash flows in FY25 were primarily due to an increase in trade receivables and other non-current financial assets, along with a decrease in other current liabilities related to the one-time intellectual property acquisition in FY24. In FY26 and the three months ended June 30, 2026, the outflows were mainly attributable to increased inventory requirements, changes in other current assets and provisions, and working capital adjustments. Continued negative operating cash flows could create liquidity challenges for the company.

The company incurred liquidated damages amounting to Rs 21.82 crore, Rs 18.93 crore, and Rs 3.80 crore in FY24, FY25, and FY26, respectively, due to delays in meeting contractual delivery schedules. Its defence contracts also contain stringent warranty obligations, and further delays or product defects could result in additional penalties and replacement costs.

The company depends significantly on its Bengaluru R&D centre, where it designs and develops pilot engineering units before outsourcing large-scale manufacturing. Any adverse political, social or economic developments in Karnataka, or disruptions at this facility, could negatively affect its product development and business operations.
As of August 31, 2026, the company had outstanding financial indebtedness of Rs 246.25 crore. Any failure to service or repay these loans can harm the company’s operations and financial position.

profile.overview:
Shellz manufactures and markets confectionery products and supplies food and bakery ingredients. Its product portfolio includes over 300 stock keeping units (SKUs) across categories such as baked treats, chocolates, jellies, panned confectionery and sugar confectionery. The company markets its consumer products under the brands Hugs and Tosca. It also manufactures products under private labels for third-party customers and exports to markets in the Middle East, South Asia, and Europe. 
In addition, it supplies non-branded food and bakery ingredients. The company operates through a distribution network of over 300 super stockists, with its products available across retail outlets in around 24 states in India as of March 31, 2026. Its manufacturing facilities are located in Delhi and Sonipat, Haryana. The Sonipat facility is being developed to consolidate and expand existing operations and increase production capacity. The company manufactures its consumer products in-house.
profile.productsAndServices: Shellz India Ltd operates in FMCG (Founded 2012).
profile.businessModel: SME issue (FP) listed on BSE · ISIN INE0Z7301016.
profile.industryOverview: FMCG primary market offering tracked via SEBI & exchange filings.
strengths: Shellz offers products across categories such as baked treats, choco delights, jellies, panned confectionery and sugar candies. It has developed products such as Dip Sticks, which combine biscuit sticks with chocolate cream, and Push Up, a cone-based cream and biscuit snack. Its Tosca brand also includes Tosca Oat Choco, an oat and cereal-based product.

A majority of the company’s SKUs are priced at Rs 10 or below. Its products cater to mass-market consumers across different consumption occasions, while the Tosca brand targets the relatively higher-priced mass-premium segment.

As of March 31, 2026, Shellz had a network of over 300 super stockists, with its products available across retail outlets in around 24 states in India. Its distribution model relies on super stockists and distributors to reach urban, semi-urban and rural markets.

The company manufactures its consumer products in-house at its production facilities in Delhi and Sonipat, Haryana. It claims that its manufacturing setup supports multiple confectionery categories and formats, with machinery sourced from countries including Turkey, China, and Indonesia. The Sonipat facility is being developed to consolidate existing operations and expand production capacity.

Shellz claims to have a team of food and packaging technologists involved in product formulation, ingredient selection, product trials, and packaging design. Its product development process includes evaluating taste, stability, manufacturability, and shelf life before commercialisation.

The company has witnessed a consistent increase in its revenue from operations and profit after tax (PAT). Revenue from operations increased from Rs 162.41 crore in FY24 to Rs 186.97 crore in FY25 and Rs 192.61 crore in FY26. PAT increased from Rs 5.25 crore in FY24 to Rs 8.30 crore in FY25 and Rs 13.37 crore in FY26.
risks: The company, its subsidiaries, group companies, promoters, directors, key managerial personnel and senior managerial personnel are involved in certain ongoing legal proceedings. Any adverse decisions in these cases could negatively affect the company’s business, results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

The company has faced litigation involving vendors and suppliers, including cases related to unpaid dues and cheque dishonour. It does not have long-term supply agreements with most suppliers and sourced raw materials from 132 suppliers in the three months ended June 30, 2026, 249 suppliers in FY26, 218 suppliers in FY25 and 212 suppliers in FY24. The company provides unsecured personal loans to salaried and self-employed individuals through its digital lending platform, on both direct lending and co-lending bases. Its lending operations are focused on borrowers in urban and semi-urban areas of India, including first-time borrowers. 
The company operates its lending business through the “LoanFront” brand and its mobile application, “LoanFront - Personal Loan App.” The app supports loan origination, due diligence, underwriting, documentation, disbursal, and repayment. Its digital infrastructure also uses verification and technology-enabled tools for credit assessment, credit decisioning, and risk evaluation. In addition to lending, the company provides application and technology services to other NBFCs. Vaibhav Vyapaar was incorporated in Kolkata, West Bengal, in 2009 and received its NBFC licence from the RBI in 2010. It has operated through the LoanFront platform since 2019.

Papadmalji Agro Foods is a food products company headquartered in Bikaner, Rajasthan, engaged in the in-house manufacturing of hand-made and machine-made papads, ready-to-fry papads, rice papads (khichiya), vrat-special papads, and moongodi. 
The company also undertakes white-label manufacturing of hand-made papads for clients, who sell the products under their own brands and packaging. In addition, it trades in cereal pellets under its own brand. Its manufacturing facilities use semi-automated and automated machinery for dough preparation, sheeting, rolling, cutting, drying, and packaging. 
The company operates under five brands: Zhakaas, Vishal, Rozana, Diamond, and Papadmalji, covering different product categories and distribution channels. Its products are sold through general trade, modern trade, quick commerce platforms, and its direct-to-consumer website. Exports are done through an independent merchant exporter, which handles exports to select Middle Eastern countries.

strengths: The company had 76 distributors and 30 wholesalers as of March 31, 2026, covering 8,710 retail outlets across multiple states. Its distributor network covered 7,470 outlets, while wholesalers covered another 1,240 outlets across regions including Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and others.

The company sells its products through multiple channels, including general trade, modern trade, quick commerce, its direct-to-consumer platform, and a merchant exporter. As of March 31, 2026, it was associated with seven modern trade channels, one quick commerce platform, and one merchant exporter serving the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait, and Bahrain.

The company has a broad product portfolio covering different types of papads and related food products. Its offerings include handmade and machine-made papads, ready-to-fry papads, rice papads, vrat-special papads, cereal pellets, and moongodi, with multiple variants under each category.

Handmade and machine-made papads together accounted for 69.19% of revenue from operations in FY26. Handmade papads contributed 41.33%, while machine-made papads contributed 27.86%. Rice papads (khichiya) contributed another 24.09% of revenue during the same period.

The company claims to use semi-automated and automated machinery for several stages of machine-made papad production. Its processes include dough preparation, sheeting, rolling, cutting, drying, and packaging, while handmade papads are produced through a network of nine Bataras who coordinate home-based papad makers.

The company has established a multi-brand portfolio covering different product categories and sales channels. Its brands include Zhakaas, Vishal, Rozana, Diamond, and Papadmalji, with products distributed through general trade, modern trade, quick commerce, merchant exporters, and its own direct-to-consumer platform.

The company has a structured model for its handmade papad production involving women working through a network of Bataras. As of the prospectus date, nine Bataras managed the distribution of raw materials, collection of finished products, and quality control among home-based papad makers.

The company has witnessed a consistent increase in its revenue from operations and profit after tax (PAT). Revenue from operations increased from Rs 26.27 crore in FY24 to Rs 31.75 crore in FY25 and Rs 33.53 crore in FY26. PAT increased from Rs 2.11 crore in FY24 to Rs 4.72 crore in FY25 and Rs 5.21 crore in FY26.
risks: The company is dependent on a limited number of customers, with its top 10 customers contributing Rs 15.41 crore (45.94%), Rs 21.99 crore (69.25%), and Rs 18.30 crore (69.65%) of revenue from operations in FY26, FY25, and FY24, respectively. Any loss, reduction, delay, or cancellation of orders from key customers could adversely affect the company’s revenue, cash flows, working capital cycle, and financial condition.

The company depends on a limited number of suppliers for its raw materials, with its top 10 suppliers accounting for Rs 13.76 crore (61.02%), Rs 11.66 crore (54.29%), and Rs 14.58 crore (67.44%) of total purchases in FY26, FY25, and FY24, respectively. The company does not have long-term supply agreements with these suppliers and purchases key raw materials based on prevailing market prices and demand. Any disruption in supply or increase in raw material prices could affect its production volumes, cost structure, profitability, and financial performance.

The company’s manufacturing units are concentrated in Bikaner, Rajasthan, exposing its operations to risks specific to the region. Extreme climatic conditions, water scarcity, natural disasters, infrastructure failures, transportation disruptions, regulatory changes, or socio-political disturbances in the area could disrupt production, delay deliveries, increase operating costs, and adversely affect the company’s business and financial condition.

The company recorded negative cash flow from operating activities of Rs 2.75 crore in FY24, compared with positive cash flows of Rs 2.42 crore and Rs 0.56 crore in FY25 and FY26, respectively. The negative cash flow in FY24 was mainly due to an increase in inventory, short-term loans and advances, other current assets, and overdue trade receivables, which the company attributes largely to business growth during the year. Sustained positive operating cash flows are important to fund the company’s day-to-day operations and growth plans without having to borrow.

The company had contingent liabilities of Rs 2.77 crore as of March 31, 2026. Any adverse outcome or materialisation of these liabilities could affect the company’s financial position, results of operations and cash flows.

The company had outstanding financial indebtedness of Rs 13.79 crore as of August 31, 2026. Any failure to service or repay its borrowings on time could adversely affect the company’s business, financial condition, and cash flows.

The company had trade receivables of Rs 3.44 crore as of March 31, 2026. Any delay or failure in collecting these receivables could increase working capital requirements and adversely affect the company’s cash flows and financial condition.

profile.overview:
VANS Electroengineerings Limited is a manufacturer of components for traction power supply and overhead equipment systems used in railway electrification, metro, and renewable energy systems. Its products are mainly supplied to Indian Railways and railway contractors. 
The company manufactures single-pole and double-pole vacuum circuit breakers and vacuum interrupters, which are used in traction substations, sectioning posts, feeding posts, and other railway electrification applications. Its product portfolio includes products approved by the Research Designs and Standards Organisation (RDSO) for specified railway applications. The company operates from its registered office and manufacturing facility in Salem, Tamil Nadu. 
The facility manufactures vacuum circuit breakers and vacuum interrupters and has machinery for processing and handling, along with in-house testing and quality control infrastructure. The company is ISO 9001:2015 certified and has received approvals from RDSO and the Central Organisation for Railways Electrification (CORE) for specified products.

profile.overview:
SRIT India Limited is a Bengaluru-headquartered information technology and IT-enabled services company providing digital solutions, system integration, and automation services. Its operations are organised across healthcare, electronic governance, and telecommunications and broadband. 
In healthcare, the company provides hospital information systems, revenue cycle management, digital health platforms, system integration, implementation, data migration, and maintenance services. Its electronic governance services include e-governance platforms, cybersecurity solutions, enterprise software and digital service delivery systems for government clients and enterprises. 
In telecommunications and broadband, it provides networking, connectivity, system integration, and managed services, including fibre optic networks, broadband infrastructure, IP-MPLS networks, and smart city infrastructure. Its delivery processes are appraised at CMMI Level 5 and SSE-CMM and certified to ISO 27034-1:2011, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and ISO 45001:2018. It has executed over 103 projects in the last decade.

blogs.excerpt: A complete guide to Mainboard and SME IPO structures, fresh issue vs Offer for Sale (OFS), book building, and the SEBI T+3 listing cycle.

toc.title: 1. What is an Initial Public Offering?
2. Fresh Issue vs. Offer for Sale (OFS)

sections.heading: 1. What is an Initial Public Offering?
paragraphs: An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is the process through which a privately held company raises equity capital from institutional and retail investors and lists its shares on stock exchanges such as the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE).

Before launching an IPO in India, the issuer files a Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), disclosing audited historical financials, business risks, promoter shareholding, and objects of the issue.

sections.heading: 2. Fresh Issue vs. Offer for Sale (OFS)
paragraphs: Understanding the split between Fresh Issue and Offer for Sale is critical to evaluating capital deployment.
bullets: Fresh Issue: New shares are created and issued; proceeds flow directly into the company for capex, debt reduction, or working capital.
Offer for Sale (OFS): Existing promoters or private equity investors sell their stake; proceeds go to the selling shareholders rather than the company balance sheet.

sections.heading: 3. Mainboard vs. SME IPO Platforms
paragraphs: Mainboard IPOs typically carry smaller retail lot sizes (~₹14,000–₹15,000 per lot) and list on NSE/BSE main boards. SME IPOs list on NSE Emerge or BSE SME with minimum retail lot sizes exceeding ₹1,00,000 and higher post-listing liquidity risk.

sections.heading: 4. The SEBI T+3 Listing Timeline
paragraphs: Under SEBI’s mandatory T+3 framework, if an issue closes on Day T, allotment is finalized on T+1, refunds/unblocking and demat credit occur on T+2, and shares commence trading on T+3.

sections.heading: 1. ASBA Bank Blocking vs. UPI Mandate
paragraphs: All IPO applications in India use ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount). Instead of debiting money upfront, your bank temporarily blocks the application amount in your savings account until allotment is finalized.
Retail applicants applying up to ₹5,00,000 can apply via broker apps using a UPI ID, provided they approve the UPI mandate request before 5:00 PM on the closing day.

sections.heading: 2. Retail, sNII, bNII & QIB Categories
paragraphs: SEBI classifies non-institutional and retail bidders strictly by application size:
bullets: Retail Individual Investor (RII): Up to ₹2,00,000 per PAN.
Big NII (bNII): Above ₹10,00,000 (must apply via bank ASBA netbanking).

sections.heading: 3. Why Cut-Off Price Matters for Retail
paragraphs: In oversubscribed book-built issues, the final issue price is almost always fixed at the upper end of the price band. Selecting the "Cut-Off Price" option ensures your bid remains valid at the final discovered price (available only to Retail and Employee categories).

blogs.title: IPO Allotment Explained: Proportional vs. Lottery Allocation & Registrar Check
blogs.seoTitle: IPO Allotment Process & How to Check Allotment Status | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: How registrars like KFinTech and Link Intime process oversubscribed IPO allotments, why single-lot applications work in Retail, and how to check status.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: Understand SEBI’s lottery allotment rule for oversubscribed Retail and sNII buckets, common rejection reasons, and official registrar verification.

sections.heading: 1. Oversubscribed Retail Lottery Rule
paragraphs: When the Retail category is subscribed more than 1x, SEBI rules mandate that every valid applicant should receive at least one minimum lot if possible. If applicants exceed available lots, the registrar runs a computerized random lottery.
Applying for multiple lots from the same PAN in an oversubscribed retail issue does not improve allotment odds compared to applying for 1 lot.

sections.heading: 2. Common Reasons Applications Get Rejected
paragraphs: Ensure technical accuracy before submitting bids:
bullets: Multiple applications submitted using the same PAN across different brokers.
UPI mandate left unapproved or expiring prior to issue closure.
Mismatch between bank account holder name/PAN and demat account PAN.

sections.heading: 3. Official Allotment Status Check
paragraphs: Always verify allotment directly on the official registrar portal (such as KFin Technologies, Link Intime, or Bigshare Services) or the NSE/BSE IPO verification pages using your PAN or Application Number.

blogs.title: IPO GMP Explained: What Grey Market Premium Means & Its Limitations
blogs.seoTitle: IPO GMP Explained – Formula, Risks & Unofficial Nature | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Learn what IPO Grey Market Premium (GMP) is, how estimated listing price is calculated, and why unofficial GMP cannot predict guaranteed listing gains.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: A transparent breakdown of how unofficial grey market premiums form, how hypothetical listing estimates are calculated, and why fundamentals matter more.

toc.title: 3. Why GMP Is Not an Exchange Quote

sections.heading: 1. What is Grey Market Premium?
paragraphs: Grey Market Premium (GMP) refers to an unofficial, unregulated over-the-counter premium or discount at which IPO shares are quoted informally before official listing on NSE or BSE.
GMP is not recognized, regulated, or published by SEBI, NSE, or BSE.

sections.heading: 2. How Hypothetical Listing Estimates Work
paragraphs: Trackers compute a hypothetical reference price using the upper price band plus the latest unofficial GMP:
bullets: Estimated Listing Price = IPO Upper Issue Price + Latest GMP
Estimated Gain % = (Latest GMP / IPO Upper Issue Price) × 100

sections.heading: 3. Why GMP Is Not an Exchange Quote
paragraphs: Grey market quotes suffer from thin liquidity, speculative sentiment swings, and zero settlement guarantee. Broad market corrections between issue close and listing day frequently cause actual exchange opening prices to diverge sharply from prior GMP expectations.

blogs.title: Fundamental Analysis & Financial Ratios: P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE & Debt-to-Equity
blogs.seoTitle: Financial Ratios for Indian Stocks – P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE Explained | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Master essential stock valuation and profitability ratios including P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE, and Debt-to-Equity when analysing NSE/BSE companies and IPOs.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: How to read company financial statements, compare valuation multiples against industry peers, and avoid value traps using capital efficiency metrics.

sections.heading: 1. Valuation Multiples: P/E and P/B
paragraphs: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) compares a company’s share price to its Earnings Per Share (EPS). Always compare a stock or IPO’s P/E against listed sector peers using the same reporting period (TTM or FY26).
Price-to-Book (P/B) is especially vital for banks, NBFCs, and asset-heavy lenders where book value reflects tangible equity capital.

sections.heading: 2. Profitability: ROE vs. ROCE
paragraphs: Return on Equity (ROE = Net Profit / Shareholders’ Equity) measures return generated on equity capital, while Return on Capital Employed (ROCE = EBIT / Capital Employed) evaluates total operational efficiency across both debt and equity.

sections.heading: 3. Balance Sheet Safety: Debt-to-Equity
paragraphs: A rising ROE fueled by excessive borrowing is fragile during interest-rate upcycles. Checking Debt-to-Equity alongside interest coverage ensures earnings growth is backed by sustainable cash flow.

blogs.title: Stock Market Basics: Understanding NSE, BSE, NIFTY 50, SENSEX & Mutual Funds
blogs.seoTitle: Indian Stock Market Basics – NSE, BSE, NIFTY 50 & Mutual Funds | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Learn how NSE and BSE operate, how NIFTY 50 and SENSEX indices are weighted, and how equity mutual funds compare to direct stock investing.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: An essential primer on India’s dual-exchange market structure, free-float market capitalization indices, order types, and diversified mutual funds.

sections.heading: 1. NSE and BSE Market Structure
paragraphs: India’s equity trading centres on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), regulated by SEBI with T+1 equity settlement. Most large-cap and mid-cap stocks trade on both exchanges simultaneously.

sections.heading: 2. How NIFTY 50 and SENSEX Work
paragraphs: NIFTY 50 tracks 50 large, liquid Indian companies weighted by free-float market capitalization, while BSE SENSEX tracks 30 blue-chip leaders. Sectoral indices such as BANK NIFTY track concentrated banking performance.

sections.heading: 3. Direct Equities vs. Mutual Funds
paragraphs: Investors seeking diversified market exposure without single-stock research overhead often combine core index or flexi-cap mutual funds (regulated under AMFI/SEBI norms) with selective direct equity or IPO allocations.

blogs.seoTitle: Stock Market & IPO Investment Risks – Risk Management Guide | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Understand market volatility, SME liquidity risk, valuation compression, and position sizing discipline for Indian retail investors.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: Why capital preservation, reading RHP risk factors, and understanding SME market-lot liquidity matter before committing capital.

sections.heading: 1. Valuation & Post-Listing Drawdown Risk
paragraphs: Not every IPO lists at a premium. Companies priced aggressively during peak market optimism can list below issue price or underperform if post-listing quarterly earnings miss prospectus projections.

sections.heading: 2. SME Board Liquidity & Circuit Limits
paragraphs: SME-listed equities trade in fixed lot sizes and often hit 5% or 20% circuit filters with thin order-book depth, making rapid exits difficult during risk-off sessions.

sections.heading: 3. Position Sizing & Verified Research
paragraphs: Always cross-verify financial statements in the official RHP/Prospectus, separate speculative GMP chatter from balance-sheet quality, and size individual equity bets conservatively within your overall asset allocation.

blogs.title: How to Read a DRHP & RHP Prospectus: 7 Critical Sections Before Applying for Any IPO
blogs.seoTitle: How to Read DRHP & RHP IPO Prospectus – Investor Checklist | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Learn which sections of a SEBI DRHP or RHP prospectus matter most: Objects of the Issue, Risk Factors, Litigations, Promoter Holding, and Restated Financials.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: Skip the 400-page overwhelm: focus on Objects of the Issue, working capital intensity, contingent liabilities, related-party transactions, and peer valuation.

toc.title: 1. Objects of the Issue & Fresh vs. OFS Split
3. Restated Cash Flows vs. Accounting Profit

sections.heading: 1. Objects of the Issue & Fresh vs. OFS Split
paragraphs: Every Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) opens with a concise summary of capital deployment. Distinguish carefully between Fresh Issue proceeds funding productive capacity or debt repayment versus Offer for Sale (OFS) exits by early financial sponsors or promoters.
Watch out for vague "General Corporate Purposes" exceeding 25% of issue proceeds or sudden pre-IPO debt spikes slated for repayment using public funds.
bullets: Check exact capex milestones and scheduled commercial operation dates.
Verify promoter lock-in periods (typically 18 months for minimum promoter contribution and 6 months for remaining pre-IPO equity).

sections.heading: 2. Material Risk Factors & Pending Litigations
paragraphs: Do not treat the Internal Risk Factors section as boilerplate. Pay close attention to customer concentration (whether Top 5 clients contribute over 50% of revenue), single-geography factory exposure, regulatory license renewals, and tax or criminal proceedings involving directors or group entities.

sections.heading: 3. Restated Cash Flows vs. Accounting Profit
paragraphs: Compare three-year Restated Consolidated PAT against Operating Cash Flow (OCF) and Trade Receivables days. A company reporting rapid profit expansion while operating cash flow remains persistently negative may face working capital stress or aggressive revenue recognition.

sections.heading: 4. Related-Party Transactions & Promoter Track Record
paragraphs: Inspect Related-Party Transactions (RPT) in the financial notes for raw-material purchases, factory lease rentals, or brand royalties paid to promoter-owned private entities. Transparent governance lowers post-listing minority shareholder risk.

blogs.title: Capital Gains Tax on IPO Listing Gains & Listed Indian Equities (STCG & LTCG Guide)
blogs.seoTitle: STCG & LTCG Tax Rules on Indian IPOs & Stocks | PriceAlerter
blogs.metaDescription: Understand how Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG), Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG), STT, holding periods, and dividend income are taxed on NSE and BSE equities in India.
blogs.author: PriceAlerter Editorial Research
blogs.excerpt: An investor reference on holding period classification (12-month threshold), listing-day sell tax implications, STT applicability, and AIS/Form 26AS reconciliation.

toc.title: 1. Holding Period: Demat Credit Date to Sell Date

sections.heading: 1. Holding Period: Demat Credit Date to Sell Date
paragraphs: For IPO shares allotted in India, the holding period for Income Tax purposes commences from the date shares are allotted/credited to your demat account, not the application bid date.
Listed equity shares sold on recognized Indian exchanges (NSE/BSE) where Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is paid qualify as Long-Term Capital Assets only if held for more than 12 months.

sections.heading: 2. Short-Term vs. Long-Term Equity Gains
paragraphs: Selling IPO shares on listing day or within 12 months triggers Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG) under Section 111A of the Income Tax Act (20% base rate plus applicable surcharge and 4% cess under post-July 2024 Finance Act rules).

Equity holdings sold after 12 months qualify for Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) under Section 112A (12.5% rate above the ₹1.25 lakh annual aggregate exemption threshold, without indexation). Always consult a qualified Chartered Accountant for your personal slab and surcharge rules.

sections.heading: 3. Dividends, STT & Tax Record-Keeping
paragraphs: Equity dividends received from NSE/BSE companies are taxable at your marginal income tax slab rate, with 10% TDS deducted when annual dividends from a company exceed statutory limits. Reconcile your broker Profit & Loss statement with the Income Tax AIS portal before filing ITR-2 or ITR-3.
